performers: Fyodor Chaliapin, bass; orchestra conducted by George W. Byng
intro: The Song of the Volga Boatmen, a song of the men who hauled barges, in an arrangement by Chaliapin and Keneman for solo bass and orchestra. Chaliapin sings, and George W. Byng conducts the orchestra.

sections.label: A · The hauling song, solo bass
sections.mNote: A solo bass sings the work song.

cues.title: Solo bass with orchestra
cues.text: Chaliapin sings a song made for a group of working men. In his arrangement with Fyodor Keneman, a single bass voice sings the repeated hauling call, sung in Russian, with orchestral accompaniment.
cues.evidence: DAHR, Victor 88663: bass solo with orchestra, sung in Russian, arranged by Chaliapin and Keneman. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/162251. The song’s origins: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_the_Volga_Boatmen

cues.title: Barge-haulers and their refrain
cues.text: The boatmen are barge-haulers, pulling from the riverbank. Their refrain, “Ey, ukhnyem!”, is the recurring hauling call. The words call for one more effort, and then another.
cues.evidence: Traditional Russian song and lyrics, collected by Mily Balakirev and published in 1866. “Ey, ukhnyem!” is the recurring hauling call. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_the_Volga_Boatmen

cues.title: Repin’s Barge Haulers on the Volga, 1873
cues.text: Repin painted the same labour in Barge Haulers on the Volga. It shows men harnessed to a towline, leaning into its pull along the riverbank. The painting dates from 1873, and Chaliapin recorded the song nearly fifty years later.
cues.evidence: Ilya Repin, Barge Haulers on the Volga (1873), reproduced with the song’s history: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Song_of_the_Volga_Boatmen. The recording date is 9 October 1922: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/162251
